{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01VPH19NBxLy6d1uy1wWyzyz","type":"tool_result","content":"# nurb design doctrine\n\nPrinted via `nurb rules`. This file is the single source; harness files point at it\nrather than repeating it.\n\nThese are standing rules for FDM-printed parts, and several are vetoes rather than\npreferences. Most of them are physics, so they outlive any particular CAD kernel. The\nones that are specific to OCCT are marked as such and were measured, not reasoned.\n\n## The part contract\n\n```python\nfrom nurb import *\n\n@part\ndef dispenser(width=80.0, height=120.0, wall=2.0, draft=False):\n    body = Box(width, height, wall)\n    if draft:\n        return body\n    bed = body.bounding_box().min.Z\n    keep = body.edges().filter_by(lambda e: e.bounding_box().min.Z > bed)\n    return polish(body, keep, 1.0)\n```\n\nKeyword defaults are the parameters. That one declaration feeds the agent, the CLI, the\nviewer, the tests, and any future configurator. Never add a parallel `PARAMS` dict; the\ntwo would drift.\n\n**Write a continuous dimension as a float.** The type of a default is the only thing\nthat says whether a value is a count or a measurement, and the viewer reads it: an `int`\ndefault gets a slider that steps by one, a `float` default one that moves continuously.\n`bracket_count=4` is a count and `chamfer_size=1.0` is a millimetre, so the trailing\n`.0` is doing work. Nothing else has to be declared, and there is no annotation to keep\nin sync, because the type is already there in the signature.\n\n`draft` is optional and injected by the runtime, never passed by a caller. When it is\ntrue, skip the polish pass. It is worth about 20% on a real part, not the 18x a cube\nsuggests.\n\nReturn one solid. A function that returns two loose bodies still reports a plausible\nbounding box and still exports, so nothing downstream catches it.\n\n## Printability\n\n- **Minimum wall 2 to 3mm**, except where fit geometry says otherwise. Fit-critical\n  dimensions are already tuned; do not round them for tidiness.\n- **Print support-free. No floating features.** Parts print bottom down, building up in\n  +z, so every functional feature is grounded. A vertical extrusion or a vertical\n  through hole is self-supporting. A shelf, loop, or band floated partway up with a gap\n  underneath is not.\n- **Corbel rule.** Grounded does not mean a column to the bed. Support-free means no\n  layer overhanging past 45 degrees. Where material would run to the plate only to\n  satisfy printing, carry the feature on a 45 degree underside instead: a short vertical\n  tip of 4 to 6mm below the floor at the front face, then a 45 degree plane falling back\n  into the body. Every layer then overhangs by at most half a bead and bonds to the wall\n  behind it.\n- **Corbels are always exactly 45 degrees**, the same as every other facet. Never\n  steepen one or match it to a ratio. Let the landing point fall where 45 degrees puts\n  it. Mismatched facet angles are a veto: every facet on the part, cosmetic or\n  structural or corbel, has to read as one system.\n- **Elephant's foot is a slicer setting**, not a CAD problem. Do not model around it.\n\n## Print orientation\n\nParts print the way they are modelled, +z up, and for most parts that is the end of it. Orientation becomes a decision in exactly two situations: an overhang a corbel cannot carry without disfiguring the part, and a load that wraps a corner, where no flat orientation keeps every member strong.\n\n- **The two remedies for an overhang finding are a corbel and a tilt.** Reach for the corbel first: it is local, it keeps the part on its natural face, and it disappears into the design. Reach for the tilt when the whole part fights the bed. An open box printed upright wants support inside; printed flat it has one huge first layer that warps and three finishes that do not match; stood on a corner at 45 degrees, nothing needs support and every face is printed as perimeters, one finish.\n- **Layer bonds are about half strength**, measured near 50% of in-plane tensile for PLA and worse for ASA. A part loaded around a corner, which is every bracket and every L, has no flat orientation that keeps both legs loading in-plane: one of them always pulls its layers apart. Stood at 45 degrees neither does, and the load path never lies in a single weld plane. A tilt moves the weak plane rather than deleting it, so it is not automatic: a hook printed at an angle fails at the same load with the break somewhere else. It earns its keep on corners, not on straight pulls.\n- **`stand(part, tilt, axis, facet)` is the verb.** It rotates the part about a horizontal axis, seats it, and shaves the down corner flat, because a part standing on an unshaved corner meets the bed along a single extrusion line, and that line peels. The facet is 2mm minimum, measured across the flat. 45 degrees is the usual tilt and is not sacred: a shallow part stands at whatever angle brings everything inside the limit. Run the polish pass before standing, in the functional orientation.\n- **Stand a part on the corner that grounds every region, and prefer the lowest stance that does.** For an L that is the outside of its elbow, legs up in a V. The sign of the roll depends on which way the model faces, so check rather than reason: the same L rolled the other way stands on the end of one leg as a chevron, still grounded, still legal, but 60% taller on the same facet, and height on a facet is what spends the adhesion margin. The stance to refuse is the tent, elbow up, one leg's tip hanging in air, and it is easy to miss by eye because nothing about it looks steep: every face of the floating tip can sit at exactly 45 degrees, silent to the overhang rule. The `floating` rule fails any region whose first layer has nothing to sit on and `stability` judges the height, so `nurb check` on the stood variant settles the corner choice. Past grounded, inside the limit, and low, the tilt is taste: what remains is where the facet scar lands, which is the user's call.\n- **A diagonal print is a variant, and it is offered, never imposed.** The facet is cut from visible geometry, and whether that corner may go is not a printability question: only the user knows whether it shows. The pattern is a bool parameter, `diagonal=False`, that applies `stand()` when true, and a card variant that sets it, so it builds, checks against its own baselines, exports its own STL and shows in the viewer like any variant. Give the variant a `note` saying what the tilt buys and costs in plain words, \"prints tilted on a flattened corner: no supports, and stronger across the corner\", never in the doctrine's. Build it speculatively and link it, `?part=x&variant=x_diagonal`; the user judges by looking, and two lines delete it if they pass.\n- **Past about twenty times the facet width in height, adhesion is holding a lever, and `stand()` grows fins.** A compact part holds its facet by first-layer adhesion; a tall one needs support fins modelled into the part, never slicer supports, whose loose grip lets warp tension spring the part free mid-print. The recipe is print-farm practice with fixed numbers, so it is generated rather than judged: a thin blade at each side of the part hugging the lean across a small gap, each on a 1mm pad for its own adhesion, joined to the part only by horizontal tines a single layer tall and a bead wide, about 0.5 x 0.5mm, five or so, biased toward the bottom where the young print is least stable. After printing the fins lift off whole and the tine stubs rub off with a fingernail. The tines cost a handful of sub-millimetre faces, declared on the card like any other earned sliver. The stability warning remains the referee for what `stand()` did not build: pass `fins=False` to see it, and a part tilted by hand still gets it.\n\n## Load path\n\nWork out where the weight sits and what it does at the mount before drawing anything.\n\n- **Shear**, a straight down load close to the wall, is handled well and rarely needs\n  reinforcement.\n- **Bending moment**, a load projecting forward, is the dominant failure mode. Load\n  times distance levers the top of the part off its mount and concentrates stress at\n  the inside corner where the platform meets the body.\n- **Lateral load and torsion** are answered by a second mount point, not by thickening.\n  A single-mount part carrying an off-center load twists.\n- **FDM is anisotropic.** Layer bonds are the weak direction and a cantilever moment\n  peels them apart. Spread load into the body with gussets rather than adding section\n  thickness.\n\n**Projection-to-height ratio** decides the reinforcement. A loaded shelf pries at the\nwall as a force couple, and those forces scale with projection divided by the height of\nthe supporting back. Doubling the height halves the pull-out force, and height in the\nwall plane is nearly free: no forward mass, almost no material.\n\n```\n<= 1.5x    chamfers only\n1.5 - 2.5x end gussets\n> 2.5x     raise the height until it is back under 2.5, then gussets\n```\n\nDo not oversize either. A light part sits near the mounting system's minimum height. An\noversized back on a small hook is wasted material and looks wrong. `nurb check` reports\nthis ratio for any part whose card names which way it reaches.\n\n### Reinforcement, in order of preference\n\n1. **Gussets**, triangular webs joining the platform top to the body front. The most\n   effective cantilever fix, because they turn bending into compression along the\n   diagonal. Depth about half the projection, height as tall as the body allows while\n   staying low. **Outer ends only, never mid-surface**: a mid-surface gusset obstructs\n   the usable area.\n2. **Inside-corner relief**, 3mm, at every load-bearing junction. Cheap, always worth it.\n3. **Ribs** under a large platform to stop plate flex, 2 to 3mm wide, front to back.\n4. **Another mount point.** When in doubt, add one. The wall interface is stronger than\n   the printed part.\n\n**Gussets are truncated quadrilaterals, never sharp triangles.** End the outer tip with\na short vertical face of about 6mm, drawn in the profile. Do not chamfer thin-web edges\nafterwards: slope chamfers leave runout slivers and tip chamfers make compound-angle\nartifacts where they meet the platform. **Shape problems on a thin web get fixed in the\nprofile, not with a dress-up feature.**\n\n## Polish pass\n\nThe polish pass runs last, after structure is finished.\n\n1. **Chamfers are the default on exposed edges**, 1mm, never below 0.8mm. A consistent\n   faceted look that prints reliably beats a fillet default.\n2. **No chamfers lying in the back face or the bottom face.** The back sits against the\n   wall and the bottom is the bed-contact face. Chamfering an edge that lies in either\n   buys nothing, and where a bottom chamfer meets another one it makes sliver facets and\n   notch points that are very hard to print.\n   **An edge that merely ends there is fine**, and this is the distinction to get right,\n   because reading the rule as \"nothing touching the bed\" throws away the vertical corner\n   chamfers, which are the most-handled edges on the part. A vertical corner's chamfer\n   stands square to the plate and the first layer keeps its full width. A *sloped* edge\n   arriving at the plate is the case that is not fine: its chamfer lands tilted and lays\n   a knife edge into the first layer. That is exactly what `bed_bevel` measures, and it\n   tells a corbel from a chamfer by reach, since a chamfer's reach is its size.\n3. **Never touch fit-critical mating geometry**: channels, dovetails, sockets, anything\n   that has to slide onto something else. Lead-in chamfers at a mating mouth sound\n   helpful and are not. They make tiny compound facets that print badly on someone\n   else's machine.\n4. **Never polish a concave edge.** A cosmetic chamfer on an inside corner adds a thin\n   wedge instead of taking a corner off: it prints as a feather edge and collects stress\n   where the part is already weakest. A concave junction that needs relieving gets a\n   deliberate 3mm structural chamfer, sized for the load, before the polish pass runs.\n   `is_convex` and `concave_edges` are in the vocabulary a part file gets, because this\n   is the one polish mistake that is invisible in code: the selector reads as an\n   ordinary exposed-edge query and the part builds, exports and prints without\n   complaint. It shipped in this library once.\n5. **Select chamfer edges by filtering, never blanket-chamfer.** Mating edges, back-face\n   edges, bottom-face edges and concave edges all have to be excluded.\n   **Filter for what must not be touched, then let the kernel refuse the rest.** A\n   chamfer call is all or nothing, so one edge that cannot land takes the whole pass\n   down, and the tempting response is to keep narrowing the set by hand until it builds.\n   That is how a part ends up with three chamfered edges out of ninety. Narrow the set\n   for reasons you can name, then chamfer greedily: try the set, and where it fails,\n   bisect and keep the halves that build. Refuse any batch that makes a face smaller\n   than the corner triangle three chamfers leave, about `0.866 * size ** 2`, since\n   anything smaller is chamfers colliding. Chamfer the original solid with the whole\n   accepted set each time, never the result of the last attempt: an edge belongs to the\n   shape it was selected from, and applying batches in sequence quietly re-chamfers the\n   first body and returns it.\n6. **No text labels on parts.** File naming carries catalog identity. There is a second\n   reason beyond taste: a glyph's outline comes from a system font, so a part with text\n   on it builds to different geometry on a different machine. The calibration coupon,\n   which needs a label because four of them come off one plate looking identical, comes\n   out at 2600.6mm3 with 88 faces on one machine and 2601.0 with 83 on another. Nothing\n   about its fit moves, but its card cannot be asserted anywhere but where it was\n   written.\n7. **Consistency is the polish.** One chamfer size across a family is what makes it read\n   as a designed system rather than a pile of prints.\n\n**Sliver check after every polish pass.** Faces under 1mm² are a polish bug unless\njustified. The only ones the doctrine allows outright are the corner triangles where\nthree 1mm chamfers meet at a convex corner, about 0.87mm². Anything else is usually\nchamfers colliding near a mating mouth, or a chamfered concave edge. A part declares the\ncount it has earned on its card, so a new one is a regression and a known one is silent.\n\n## Kernel rules\n\nSpecific to OCCT, and measured on real parts rather than reasoned about.\n\n- **Two chamfered convex edges need more than `2 * chamfer_size` of face between them.**\n  Closer and OCCT raises `BRep_API: command not done`, which build123d surfaces as\n  \"Failed creating a chamfer, try a smaller length value(s)\". At 1mm the shelf fails\n  with 1.66mm between the edges and builds with 2.16mm; at 0.5mm it builds with 1.16mm.\n  The threshold tracks the chamfer exactly. This is the single most common way a part\n  stops building, so `chamfer` says this much at the point of failure rather than\n  leaving the kernel's advice to stand: taking \"try a smaller length\" at its word is how\n  a part ends up with a 0.4mm chamfer that lands and then prints as a defect.\n- **One chamfered edge needs more than `chamfer_size` of face**, which is the same rule\n  with one chamfer instead of two and is easy to miss because it looks like plenty of\n  room. It bites wherever a polished edge sits beside something that is never polished:\n  a concave junction, a structural chamfer's toe, a pocket wall. Measured on three\n  different parts, all at the same threshold: 1.08mm builds and 1.00mm fails at a 1mm\n  chamfer.\n- **A batch chamfer failure is not a bad edge.** Every edge in a failing set chamfers\n  fine on its own, so testing them one at a time reports that nothing is wrong. Bisect\n  the set pairwise instead. \"Try a smaller length\" would never have found the rule above.\n- **The second way a chamfer dies, where bisecting does not help**, is an edge whose end\n  lands on a vertex with four faces around it and only three edges between them. Two of\n  those faces touch at a point without sharing an edge, and OCCT has no cap for that\n  corner. The edge fails on its own, on a clean body, at every length down to 0.05mm, so\n  nothing about the failure looks like a clearance problem. The fix is to chamfer in two\n  passes so that the first one gives those two faces a real edge to meet along, then\n  reselect from the result. Found on the parts bin, where the front drop and the side\n  taper land at the same height by design.\n- **Prefer `new_edges` over geometric selectors.** Each chamfer changes topology, so a\n  selector resolved against pristine geometry drifts once an earlier chamfer runs.\n  `new_edges(before, combined=after)` returns exactly the edges an operation created. It\n  is the algebra-mode equivalent of a builder's `Select.LAST`, and algebra mode is what a\n  part file uses, so `part.edges() - last` is not available. It is what makes a part\n  survive flexing its counts.\n- **A Fusion workaround is sometimes a real constraint wearing a disguise.** The gusset\n  drop that existed only to escape `ASM_BL_NO_MATE` turned out to be the same \"a chamfer\n  needs room to land\" constraint at a different number. Deleting it would have been\n  wrong; restating it as a rule was right.\n\n## Cards\n\nA part file carries geometry, not rationale. Every part worth keeping has a card next to\nit, same basename. **Read the card before editing the part, and update it when done.**\n\nFour sections, and one of them does work nothing else does:\n\n- `## What it is`\n- `## Design notes`, why the key dimensions are what they are\n- `## Don't`, **required**, what was tried and rejected. Geometry records what is; only\n  this records what is deliberately absent. Without it an agent helpfully re-adds the\n  lead-in chamfer that was retired on purpose.\n- `## Changelog`, dated\n\nPlus two machine-facing pieces:\n\n- The **AUTO block**, regenerated by `nurb card`. Never hand-edit it. It is a cache, not\n  a source of truth, and it holds no timestamp so regenerating it on unchanged geometry\n  produces no diff.\n- The **accepted baselines**, a TOML fence carrying what this part has already justified:\n  its sliver count, its real minimum wall, its printer settings. The number goes next to\n  the sentence that earns it, because a count on its own is a magic number. Machine facts\n  stay out of it: a bed size belongs to the machine, so it lives in `printer.toml` at the\n  project root, which names a shipped profile (`profile = \"bambu_a1_mini\"`) and can\n  override any check setting machine-wide.\n\n```toml\n[part]\nmin_wall = 1.0\nforward = [-1, 0, 0]\n\n[accepted]\nsliver = 6\n```\n\n### Variants\n\nA catalog entry that is the same function at different numbers is a variant, not a new\nfile. It goes in the same fence, and `build`, `check`, `card` and `export` all walk it\nexactly as they walk the part's own defaults, so it gets its own STL, its own baselines\nand its own line in the AUTO block.\n\n```toml\n[variants.shelf_gridfinity_3x2]\nnote = \"The same shelf sized for the wide bin: three columns instead of two.\"\n\n[variants.shelf_gridfinity_3x2.params]\ngrid_x = 3\nbracket_count = 6\n\n[variants.shelf_gridfinity_3x2.accepted]\nsliver = 26\n```\n\nThe test is whether it is the same geometry. A wider cradle on the same J is a variant.\nA different mechanism is a part, however similar the slab looks.\n\n`note` is one sentence saying why the variant exists, written in the user's words rather than the doctrine's, because the viewer shows it next to the variant and its reader is whoever is about to print the thing. The params are the how and never the why: `diagonal = true` explains nothing to someone who has not read the doctrine, and \"prints tilted so it needs no supports\" does.\n\n## Measurements\n\nThe bottleneck on a one-off is not geometry, it is dimensions. A wrong number produces a\nperfect model of the wrong object, and nothing downstream can catch it.\n\n**Ask for a measurement. The\nones that are specific to OCCT are marked as such and were measured, not reasoned.\n\n## The part contract\n\n```python\nfrom nurb import *\n\n@part\ndef dispenser(width=80.0, height=120.0, wall=2.0, draft=False):\n    body = Box(width, height, wall)\n    if draft:\n        return body\n    bed = body.bounding_box().min.Z\n    keep = body.edges().filter_by(lambda e: e.bounding_box().min.Z > bed)\n    return polish(body, keep, 1.0)\n```\n\nKeyword defaults are the parameters. A shelf, loop, or band floated partway up with a gap\n  underneath is not.\n- **Corbel rule.** Grounded does not mean a column to the bed. Support-free means no\n  layer overhanging past 45 degrees. Where material would run to the plate only to\n  satisfy printing, carry the feature on a 45 degree underside instead: a short vertical\n  tip of 4 to 6mm below the floor at the front face, then a 45 degree plane falling back\n  into the body. Every layer then overhangs by at most half a bead and bonds to the wall\n  behind it.\n- **Corbels are always exactly 45 degrees**, the same as every other facet. Never\n  steepen one or match it to a ratio. Let the landing point fall where 45 degrees puts\n  it. Orientation becomes a decision in exactly two situations: an overhang a corbel cannot carry without disfiguring the part, and a load that wraps a corner, where no flat orientation keeps every member strong.\n\n- **The two remedies for an overhang finding are a corbel and a tilt.** Reach for the corbel first: it is local, it keeps the part on its natural face, and it disappears into the design. Reach for the tilt when the whole part fights the bed. An open box printed upright wants support inside; printed flat it has one huge first layer that warps and three finishes that do not match; stood on a corner at 45 degrees, nothing needs support and every face is printed as perimeters, one finish.\n- **Layer bonds are about half strength**, measured near 50% of in-plane tensile for PLA and worse for ASA. A part loaded around a corner, which is every bracket and every L, has no flat orientation that keeps both legs loading in-plane: one of them always pulls its layers apart. Stood at 45 degrees neither does, and the load path never lies in a single weld plane. A tilt moves the weak plane rather than deleting it, so it is not automatic: a hook printed at an angle fails at the same load with the break somewhere else. It earns its keep on corners, not on straight pulls.\n- **`stand(part, tilt, axis, facet)` is the verb.** It rotates the part about a horizontal axis, seats it, and shaves the down corner flat, because a part standing on an unshaved corner meets the bed along a single extrusion line, and that line peels. The sweep refuses any intersection that\nis not a subset of its inputs and names the solid to fix, but the fix is to model the\nobstacle as something with honest volume in the first place.\n\n**Tangent is clear, and clear is not clearance.** Collision is intersection volume, so\ntwo faces that kiss at zero volume pass, the closed door resting on its stop included.\nIn plastic a zero-clearance pass is already a bind. The declared range should carry\nthe same honesty about clearance that a tongue's `fit` carries about width.\n\n**The stop the sweep finds can be the detent the design wants.** The door that\nmotivated all of this rests open at 240 degrees against the back of its own mount,\nheld there by gravity, and that contact is a feature with a card entry, not a finding\nto engineer away. Read a jam before redesigning around it.\n\n**Never trust a swing worked out by hand.** The same hinge was hand-modelled three\ntimes and gave three answers, one of them \"impossible\"; the wrong one ran a convex\ntest against a non-convex profile, which is exactly the kind of quiet modelling error\na kernel boolean cannot make. The sweep is the authority, and it is cheap.\n\nOne hinge sweeps at a time; the others hold their pose, which is the conservative\nreading of a mechanism you can only move one hand at a time. Printability rules stay\noff assemblies entirely: each part already answered them alone, and overhang measured\non an assembled scene reports confident nonsense.\n\n## Verification\n\n\"It built\" is not verification. `nurb verify` runs the machine-checkable part of\nthis list: one solid per configuration, every count flexed upward, the rules clean,\nand the card agreeing with the geometry. The two it cannot do are the two that need\nyou, and they are items 2 and 6.\n\nBefore presenting a part:\n\n1. **Flex the driving parameters up as well as down**, for example 4 to 6 to 2 to 4.\n   Growth is what catches a frozen selector; shrinking alone passes a broken part.\n2. **Check fit-critical faces by coordinate** after any polish or resize. `nurb inspect`\n   lists them, with each finding resolved to the face it fired on. Which faces are\n   fit-critical is still yours to know, which is why this is not something `nurb verify`\n   can run for you.\n3. **Confirm the solid count**, which is almost always one.\n4. **Run `nurb check`.** Zero findings is the bar, and a finding fired at a part that\n   prints fine is a bug in the rule, not something to accept quietly.\n5. **Predict a baseline before you look at it.** Working out what the sliver count\n   should be from the polish exclusions turns the number into a test of the rule instead\n   of something to write down.\n6. **Render it and actually look.** `nurb render <part>` writes a PNG. A part can pass\n   every numeric check and still be visibly wrong.","stderr":"","interrupted":false,"isImage":false,"noOutputExpected":false}}

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01Xcc1QgPkAMdVhwan5f3Ued","type":"tool_result","content":"total 0\ndrwxr-xr-x@ 3 <user>  staff   96 Aug  1 20:31 .\ndrwxr-xr-x@ 6 <user>  staff  192 Aug  2 18:56 ..\n-rw-r--r--@ 1 <user>  staff    0 Aug  1 20:31 .gitkeep\nparts/.gitkeep\n# nurb\n\nA part is a Python function and its keyword defaults are its parameters. A project is any directory with a `parts/` folder; there is no init step. You are the CAD operator: the user describes the part and you do everything else, including creating the project and modelling.\n\n**Start `nurb dev` in the background and hand the user its URL before anything else.** It prints one, and the viewer it serves is where the user watches the part take shape: every save rebuilds and repaints without moving their camera. When your shell runs on the user's own machine, `--open` puts the viewer on their screen without the URL hop. So work in saves, not in silence. `nurb new` already emits a working part; put that blocky draft on screen in the first minute and refine it while they watch. Caption it when you hand the URL over: a user who opens the viewer to an unannounced block cannot tell the placeholder from the design, and one sentence saying it is the starting shape you are now replacing turns the same block into progress. Ten correct but invisible minutes of modelling read as a hang. And repeat the URL at the end of every reply, the handoff included: chat scrolls the link away, and a part the user was never pointed at is a part they cannot judge. The URL deep-links: `?part=<name>` opens on that part and `&variant=<name>` loads one of its card variants, so link the exact thing you changed rather than making the user find it in the list.\n\n**When `nurb dev` says something is out of date, fix it before modelling.** Its startup lines carry the version check: a `nurb update` line means the package is old, and a `nurb skill --sync` line means this very file is older than the installed nurb. Run the named command and tell the user, and after a sync re-read the skill file, because the stale copy is the one you are working from.\n\n**Offer the permission allowlist before the prompts start.** A session is dozens of `nurb` invocations and part-file saves, and a harness that asks about each one turns twenty unattended minutes into twenty check-ins the user has to keep coming back for. If your harness keeps a per-project allowlist (in Claude Code it is `.claude/settings.local.json`), offer at the start of the first session in a project to add what the loop needs, merging with anything already there, and move on without it if the user declines:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"permissions\": {\n    \"allow\": [\n      \"Bash(nurb:*)\",\n      \"Edit(parts/**)\",\n      \"Edit(measurements.toml)\",\n      \"Edit(printer.toml)\"\n    ]\n  }\n}\n```\n\nOther harnesses take the same two grants, the `nurb` prefix and edits under `parts/`, in their own file: Codex a `prefix_rule` in `.codex/rules/`, Gemini `tools.allowed` in `.gemini/settings.json`, Cursor's CLI a `Shell(nurb)` entry in `.cursor/cli.json`, OpenCode a `permission` block in `opencode.json`. Amp never prompts, so there is nothing to offer.\n\n**Run `nurb rules` before you design.** It prints the doctrine: printability, load paths, the polish pass, the kernel traps, card discipline, and what to verify. This file stays thin on purpose so there is one copy of that, in the package, which cannot drift.\n\n**Ask the tool before you read its source.** `nurb api` prints the vocabulary a part file gets, with signatures, so finding out what `concave_edges` returns is one command rather than a trip into site-packages. `nurb inspect <part>` measures a built one: face areas, normals, which faces sit on the bed, every concave edge, and each finding resolved to the face it fired on, in the units the rules report. Between them they answer the questions that otherwise become a throwaway probe script apiece, which is the most expensive habit in this loop.\n\n**Ask before you model.** Anything the part has to fit (an opening, a bracket, the object it holds) is a question for the user: ask for those measurements in one batch, up front, using your harness's question tool if it has one, and record the answers in `measurements.toml` the way the doctrine describes. Anything that is taste rather than fit becomes a parameter instead of a question, because the viewer's sliders are how the user answers those. A guessed proportion costs one slider drag; a guessed clearance prints the wrong part.\n\n**Name parameters in the user's words, because the names are the sliders.** Every keyword default shows up in the viewer labelled exactly as you spelled it, and a user staring at `pilot_dia` or `tip_boss` can only learn what it moves by dragging it and guessing. Prefer plain words over trade vocabulary (`screw_hole_width`, not `pilot_dia`; `bar_thickness`, not `bar`), say what the dimension is of, and keep a term of art only when the user said it first. Two or three words is still short; a name that needs the user to know machining jargon is a label in the wrong language. And a name is still only a label: give each parameter a one-line `name: what it moves` description in the function's docstring (`shelf_depth: how far the shelf sticks out from the wall`), because the viewer shows that line when the user hovers the slider, and it is how a control explains itself without you in the room.\n\n**When parts have to work together, assemble them before printing either.** A part that mounts to another, or moves against one, gets an `@assembly`: a function in `parts/` that returns placed solids, with `use()` building the siblings, `hinge()` declaring how one moves, and `obstacle()` standing in for the machine or wall they mount into. `nurb check` then sweeps each joint through its declared range and reports the angle where it jams and where the contact is, which is the one failure no per-part check can see: a door that builds clean, checks clean, prints beautifully and will not open. The joint angle is a keyword default, so the viewer's slider swings the assembly live for the user. Model obstacles from the user's measurements, and say on the assembly's card how rough they are.\n\n**Finish with the polish pass.** Chamfered edges are what make a print feel designed rather than extruded, so the doctrine's last step (`polish`, 1mm on exposed edges) stays in the part through every edit; the template `nurb new` emits already ends with it. Say so when you hand the part over, because the user can only ask for sharp edges if they know the chamfers are there on purpose. The viewer builds polished by default, and its polish button flips to the faster draft build.\n\n**The user does not know what they can ask for, so teach the viewer one affordance at a time.** Most users have never driven CAD through chat: they do not realize \"make it chunkier\" or \"it sags when I load it\" is a complete instruction, so end every handoff with one sentence of what they can do next: drag the sliders, hit stl to print at the current values, or say what feels wrong in plain words. Beyond that standing close, at most one tip per reply, and only at the event that makes it relevant: the first taste parameter is the moment for \"that is a slider, and when you find a setting you like, the write button makes it the part's new default\"; a part that grows an interior is the moment for the section button; the end of a session is the moment for viewer.command, the double-click that reopens all of this without you. A tip at its moment reads as guidance; the same tip a reply earlier reads as noise, and every feature at once is a manual nobody asked for.\n\n**Write the card before you hand the part over, even for a single part.** A part gets printed, used, and then revisited weeks later to adjust something, and by then the session that built it is gone. `## Don't` is the only record of what was tried and rejected, so without it the next agent helpfully re-adds the lead-in chamfer that was retired on purpose. There is no one-off: there is the first session and the ones after it, and the card is what you are leaving for them.","is_error":false}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"029d1879-f399-4a4c-8728-493eb7e6a707","uuid":"9505fea6-489e-4507-bd3d-a62a176b4fe7","timestamp":"2026-08-02T23:57:06.922Z","tool_use_result":{"stdout":"total 0\ndrwxr-xr-x@ 3 <user>  staff   96 Aug  1 20:31 .\ndrwxr-xr-x@ 6 <user>  staff  192 Aug  2 18:56 ..\n-rw-r--r--@ 1 <user>  staff    0 Aug  1 20:31 .gitkeep\nparts/.gitkeep\n# nurb\n\nA part is a Python function and its keyword defaults are its parameters. The viewer builds polished by default, and its polish button flips to the faster draft build.\n\n**The user does not know what they can ask for, so teach the viewer one affordance at a time.** Most users have never driven CAD through chat: they do not realize \"make it chunkier\" or \"it sags when I load it\" is a complete instruction, so end every handoff with one sentence of what they can do next: drag the sliders, hit stl to print at the current values, or say what feels wrong in plain words. Beyond that standing close, at most one tip per reply, and only at the event that makes it relevant: the first taste parameter is the moment for \"that is a slider, and when you find a setting you like, the write button makes it the part's new default\"; a part that grows an interior is the moment for the section button; the end of a session is the moment for viewer.command, the double-click that reopens all of this without you. A tip at its moment reads as guidance; the same tip a reply earlier reads as noise, and every feature at once is a manual nobody asked for.\n\n**Write the card before you hand the part over, even for a single part.** A part gets printed, used, and then revisited weeks later to adjust something, and by then the session that built it is gone. `## Don't` is the only record of what was tried and rejected, so without it the next agent helpfully re-adds the lead-in chamfer that was retired on purpose. There is no one-off: there is the first session and the ones after it, and the card is what you are leaving for them.","stderr":"","interrupted":false,"isImage":false,"noOutputExpected":false}}

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01QVYzJuUj2TQxtKMj7uohRq","type":"tool_result","content":"  parts/cable_clip.py\n  parts/cable_clip.md\n--- PY ---\nfrom nurb import *\n\n\n@part\ndef cable_clip(width=40.0, depth=30.0, height=20.0, wall=2.0, draft=False):\n    body = Box(width, depth, height)\n    if draft:\n        return body\n    # Name what must stay sharp, then let `polish` chamfer whatever the kernel takes.\n    # A bare `chamfer(...)` is all or nothing: one edge that cannot land loses the lot.\n    bed = body.bounding_box().min.Z\n    keep = body.edges().filter_by(lambda e: e.bounding_box().min.Z > bed)\n    return polish(body, keep, 1.0)\n--- MD ---\n# cable_clip\n\n## What it is\n\n## Design notes\n\n## Don't\n\n## Changelog","is_error":false}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"029d1879-f399-4a4c-8728-493eb7e6a707","uuid":"b202fdc4-ec9f-4266-ae4d-20747d7d00b3","timestamp":"2026-08-02T23:58:05.762Z","tool_use_result":{"stdout":"  parts/cable_clip.py\n  parts/cable_clip.md\n--- PY ---\nfrom nurb import *\n\n\n@part\ndef cable_clip(width=40.0, depth=30.0, height=20.0, wall=2.0, draft=False):\n    body = Box(width, depth, height)\n    if draft:\n        return body\n    # Name what must stay sharp, then let `polish` chamfer whatever the kernel takes.\n    # A bare `chamfer(...)` is all or nothing: one edge that cannot land loses the lot.\n    bed = body.bounding_box().min.Z\n    keep = body.edges().filter_by(lambda e: e.bounding_box().min.Z > bed)\n    return polish(body, keep, 1.0)\n--- MD ---\n# cable_clip\n\n## What it is\n\n## Design notes\n\n## Don't\n\n## Changelog","stderr":"","interrupted":false,"isImage":false,"noOutputExpected":false}}

{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5","id":"msg_011Cdeq1htHzXaMGNfphEYFQ","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_01Nn7bgvnoDGtbpFiYzw5SZw","name":"Write","input":{"file_path":"/var/folders/s4/by90nw7j7_l_nvvqs3hd9mjh0000gn/T/nurb-eval-trial-foh7nmqk/project/parts/cable_clip.py","content":"from nurb import *\n\nCHAMFER = 1.0\nTOL = 1e-6\n\n\n@part\ndef cable_clip(\n    bundle_diameter=measured(\"bundle_diameter\"),\n    cable_clearance=0.4,\n    wall_thickness=2.4,\n    base_thickness=3.0,\n    clip_length=12.0,\n    tab_length=10.0,\n    screw_hole_width=4.2,\n    draft=False,\n):\n    \"\"\"A screw-down clip: the bundle drops into an open-top channel, one screw holds it.\n\n    bundle_diameter: how thick the cable bundle is across\n    cable_clearance: how much wider than the bundle the channel is cut\n    wall_thickness: how thick each channel wall is\n    base_thickness: how thick the floor under the cable is, and the mounting tab\n    clip_length: how far the clip runs along the cable\n    tab_length: how far the mounting tab sticks out past the wall\n    screw_hole_width: how wide the screw hole through the tab is\n    \"\"\"\n    channel_width = bundle_diameter + cable_clearance\n    channel_depth = bundle_diameter\n    body_width = channel_width + 2 * wall_thickness\n    body_height = base_thickness + channel_depth\n\n    corner = (Align.MIN, Align.MIN, Align.MIN)\n\n    body = Box(body_width, clip_length, body_height, align=corner)\n    # Open at the top and at both ends: the cable lies along Y through the whole part.\n    channel = Box(channel_width, clip_length + 2, channel_depth + 1, align=corner).translate(\n        (wall_thickness, -1, base_thickness)\n    )\n    tab = Box(tab_length, clip_length, base_thickness, align=corner).translate((body_width, 0, 0))\n\n    screw_x = body_width + tab_length / 2\n    screw_y = clip_length / 2\n    screw = Cylinder(screw_hole_width / 2, base_thickness + 2, align=corner).translate(\n        (screw_x, screw_y, -1)\n    )\n\n    solid = (body - channel) + tab - screw\n\n    if draft:\n        return solid\n\n    bed = solid.bounding_box().min.Z\n    concave = set(concave_edges(solid))\n\n    def keepable(e):\n        bb = e.bounding_box()\n        if e in concave:\n            return False\n        # Nothing lying in the bed face: a chamfer there buys nothing and slivers.\n        if bb.max.Z <= bed + TOL:\n            return False\n        # Nothing on the channel: its floor stays one flat face and its walls stay\n        # square, because the bundle sits against them.\n        if (\n            bb.min.X >= wall_thickness - TOL\n            and bb.max.X <= wall_thickness + channel_width + TOL\n            and bb.min.Z >= base_thickness - TOL\n        ):\n            return False\n        # Nothing on the screw hole: a lead-in there is fit geometry, not polish.\n        reach = max(\n            abs(x - screw_x) + abs(y - screw_y)\n            for x in (bb.min.X, bb.max.X)\n            for y in (bb.min.Y, bb.max.Y)\n        )\n        if reach <= screw_hole_width + TOL:\n            return False\n        return True\n\n    keep = solid.edges().filter_by(keepable)\n    return polish(solid, keep, CHAMFER)\n"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":4533,"cache_read_input_tokens":42654,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":0,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":4533},"output_tokens":6,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"not_available"},"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"029d1879-f399-4a4c-8728-493eb7e6a707","uuid":"af967305-6005-40ac-967f-6ec12cabd350","timestamp":"2026-08-02T23:58:18.748Z","request_id":"req_011Cdeq1gnpM7S15A9PoBpYn"}

{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5","id":"msg_011Cdeq2vfWyenkMtHgKGma9","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_01TQnD4uAgRMQABFLk4T8S3v","name":"Write","input":{"file_path":"/var/folders/s4/by90nw7j7_l_nvvqs3hd9mjh0000gn/T/nurb-eval-trial-foh7nmqk/project/parts/cable_clip.py","content":"from nurb import *\n\nCHAMFER = 1.0\nTOL = 1e-6\n\n\n@part\ndef cable_clip(\n    bundle_diameter=measured(\"bundle_diameter\"),\n    cable_clearance=0.4,\n    wall_thickness=2.4,\n    base_thickness=3.0,\n    clip_length=12.0,\n    tab_length=10.0,\n    screw_hole_width=4.2,\n    draft=False,\n):\n    \"\"\"A screw-down clip: the bundle drops into an open-top channel, one screw holds it.\n\n    bundle_diameter: how thick the cable bundle is across\n    cable_clearance: how much wider than the bundle the channel is cut\n    wall_thickness: how thick each channel wall is\n    base_thickness: how thick the floor under the cable is, and the mounting tab\n    clip_length: how far the clip runs along the cable\n    tab_length: how far the mounting tab sticks out past the wall\n    screw_hole_width: how wide the screw hole through the tab is\n    \"\"\"\n    channel_width = bundle_diameter + cable_clearance\n    channel_depth = bundle_diameter\n    body_width = channel_width + 2 * wall_thickness\n    body_height = base_thickness + channel_depth\n\n    corner = (Align.MIN, Align.MIN, Align.MIN)\n\n    body = Box(body_width, clip_length, body_height, align=corner)\n    # Open at the top and at both ends: the cable lies along Y through the whole part.\n    channel = Box(channel_width, clip_length + 2, channel_depth + 1, align=corner).translate(\n        (wall_thickness, -1, base_thickness)\n    )\n    tab = Box(tab_length, clip_length, base_thickness, align=corner).translate((body_width, 0, 0))\n\n    screw_x = body_width + tab_length / 2\n    screw_y = clip_length / 2\n    screw = Cylinder(screw_hole_width / 2, base_thickness + 2, align=corner).translate(\n        (screw_x, screw_y, -1)\n    )\n\n    solid = (body - channel) + tab - screw\n\n    if draft:\n        return solid\n\n    bed = solid.bounding_box().min.Z\n    concave = set(concave_edges(solid))\n\n    def keepable(e):\n        bb = e.bounding_box()\n        if e in concave:\n            return False\n        # Nothing lying in the bed face: a chamfer there buys nothing and slivers.\n        if bb.max.Z <= bed + TOL:\n            return False\n        # Nothing on the channel: its floor stays one flat face and its walls stay\n        # Nothing on the screw hole: a lead-in there is fit geometry, not polish.\n        reach = max(\n            abs(x - screw_x) + abs(y - screw_y)\n            for x in (bb.min.X, bb.max.X)\n            for y in (bb.min.Y, bb.max.Y)\n        )\n        if reach <= screw_hole_width + TOL:\n            return False\n        return True\n\n    keep = solid.edges().filter_by(keepable)\n    return polish(solid, keep, CHAMFER)\n"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":361,"cache_read_input_tokens":48536,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":0,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":361},"output_tokens":66,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"not_available"},"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"029d1879-f399-4a4c-8728-493eb7e6a707","uuid":"7f4af2f6-4eb7-41a3-b050-eac0dc5d0ff6","timestamp":"2026-08-02T23:58:33.594Z","request_id":"req_011Cdeq2uKuRdxRiJgqN2VVt"}

Open at the top and at both ends: the cable lies along Y through the whole part.\n    channel = Box(channel_width, clip_length + 2, channel_depth + 1, align=corner).translate(\n        (wall_thickness, -1, base_thickness)\n    )\n    tab = Box(tab_length, clip_length, base_thickness, align=corner).translate((body_width, 0, 0))\n\n    screw_x = body_width + tab_length / 2\n    screw_y = clip_length / 2\n    screw = Cylinder(screw_hole_width / 2, base_thickness + 2, align=corner).translate(\n        (screw_x, screw_y, -1)\n    )\n\n    solid = (body - channel) + tab - screw\n\n    if draft:\n        return solid\n\n    bed = solid.bounding_box().min.Z\n    concave = set(concave_edges(solid))\n\n    def keepable(e):\n        bb = e.bounding_box()\n        if e in concave:\n            return False\n        # Nothing lying in the bed face: a chamfer there buys nothing and slivers.\n        if bb.max.Z <= bed + TOL:\n            return False\n        # Nothing on the channel: its floor stays one flat face and its walls stay\n        # square, because the bundle sits against them.\n        if (\n            bb.min.X >= wall_thickness - TOL\n            and bb.max.X <= wall_thickness + channel_width + TOL\n            and bb.min.Z >= base_thickness - TOL\n        ):\n            return False\n        # Nothing on the screw hole: a lead-in there is fit geometry, not polish.\n        reach = max(\n            abs(x - screw_x) + abs(y - screw_y)\n            for x in (bb.min.X, bb.max.X)\n            for y in (bb.min.Y, bb.max.Y)\n        )\n        if reach <= screw_hole_width + TOL:\n            return False\n        return True\n\n    keep = solid.edges().filter_by(keepable)\n    return polish(solid, keep, CHAMFER)\n","structuredPatch":[{"oldStart":41,"oldLines":9,"newStart":41,"newLines":11,"lines":[" ","     screw_x = body_width + tab_length / 2","     screw_y = clip_length / 2","-    screw = Cylinder(screw_hole_width / 2, base_thickness + 2, align=corner).translate(","-        (screw_x, screw_y, -1)","-    )","+    screw = Cylinder(","+        screw_hole_width / 2,","+        base_thickness + 2,","+        align=(Align.CENTER, Align.CENTER, Align.MIN),","+    ).translate((screw_x, screw_y, -1))"," ","     solid = (body - channel) + tab - screw"," "]}],"userModified":false,"replaceAll":false}}

{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5","id":"msg_011CdeqZwLKCzEYJToujeZpJ","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_01GRc6ApqNy8HTr82zg35on6","name":"Write","input":{"file_path":"/var/folders/s4/by90nw7j7_l_nvvqs3hd9mjh0000gn/T/nurb-eval-trial-foh7nmqk/project/parts/cable_clip.py","content":"from nurb import *\n\nCHAMFER = 1.0\nTOL = 1e-6\n\n\n@part\ndef cable_clip(\n    bundle_diameter=measured(\"bundle_diameter\"),\n    cable_clearance=0.4,\n    wall_thickness=2.4,\n    base_thickness=3.0,\n    clip_length=12.0,\n    tab_length=10.0,\n    screw_hole_width=4.2,\n    draft=False,\n):\n    \"\"\"A screw-down clip: the bundle drops into an open-top channel, one screw holds it.\n\n    bundle_diameter: how thick the cable bundle is across\n    cable_clearance: how much wider than the bundle the channel is cut\n    wall_thickness: how thick each channel wall is\n    base_thickness: how thick the floor under the cable is, and the mounting tab\n    clip_length: how far the clip runs along the cable\n    tab_length: how far the mounting tab sticks out past the wall\n    screw_hole_width: how wide the screw hole through the tab is\n    \"\"\"\n    channel_width = bundle_diameter + cable_clearance\n    channel_depth = bundle_diameter\n    body_width = channel_width + 2 * wall_thickness\n    body_height = base_thickness + channel_depth\n\n    corner = (Align.MIN, Align.MIN, Align.MIN)\n\n    body = Box(body_width, clip_length, body_height, align=corner)\n    # Open at the top and at both ends: the cable lies along Y through the whole part,\n    # and the cut runs past both end faces so the boolean has no coincident faces.\n    channel = Box(channel_width, clip_length + 2, channel_depth + 1, align=corner).translate(\n        (wall_thickness, -1, base_thickness)\n    )\n    tab = Box(tab_length, clip_length, base_thickness, align=corner).translate((body_width, 0, 0))\n\n    screw_x = body_width + tab_length / 2\n    screw_y = clip_length / 2\n    screw_radius = screw_hole_width / 2\n    screw = Cylinder(\n        screw_radius,\n        base_thickness + 2,\n        align=(Align.CENTER, Align.CENTER, Align.MIN),\n    ).translate((screw_x, screw_y, -1))\n\n    solid = (body - channel) + tab - screw\n\n    if draft:\n        return solid\n\n    bed = solid.bounding_box().min.Z\n    concave = set(concave_edges(solid))\n\n    def keepable(e):\n        bb = e.bounding_box()\n        if e in concave:\n            return False\n        # Nothing lying in the bed face: a chamfer there buys nothing and slivers.\n        # A vertical corner that merely ends on the bed is still fair game.\n        if bb.max.Z <= bed + TOL:\n            return False\n        # Nothing on the channel. The bundle beds against the floor and both walls, so\n        # they stay square: floor one flat face the full width, walls full height.\n        if (\n            bb.min.X >= wall_thickness - TOL\n            and bb.max.X <= wall_thickness + channel_width + TOL\n            and bb.min.Z >= base_thickness - TOL\n        ):\n            return False\n        # Nothing on the screw hole: a lead-in there is fit geometry, not polish.\n        if (\n            max(abs(bb.min.X - screw_x), abs(bb.max.X - screw_x)) <= screw_radius + TOL\n            and max(abs(bb.min.Y - screw_y), abs(bb.max.Y - screw_y)) <= screw_radius + TOL\n        ):\n            return False\n        # Nothing running across the part at either end. Across the wall tops such an\n        # edge is the channel mouth, where a lead-in is forbidden outright; across the\n        # tab it would land a third chamfer on corners that already have two, and three\n        # chamfers meeting leave a facet under a square millimetre.\n        if bb.max.Y - bb.min.Y <= TOL and bb.max.Z - bb.min.Z <= TOL:\n            return False\n        return True\n\n    keep = solid.edges().filter_by(keepable)\n    return polish(solid, keep, CHAMFER)\n"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":5617,"cache_read_input_tokens":76443,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":0,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":5617},"output_tokens":3,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"not_available"},"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"029d1879-f399-4a4c-8728-493eb7e6a707","uuid":"45ccc2e4-e624-4865-a323-a9ee2f9c31a3","timestamp":"2026-08-03T00:06:06.059Z","request_id":"req_011CdeqZuFZ1Xov2cA1nL64A"}

bb.min.Y <= TOL and bb.max.Z - bb.min.Z <= TOL:","+            return False","         return True"," ","     keep = solid.edges().filter_by(keepable)"]}],"originalFile":"from nurb import *\n\nCHAMFER = 1.0\nTOL = 1e-6\n\n\n@part\ndef cable_clip(\n    bundle_diameter=measured(\"bundle_diameter\"),\n    cable_clearance=0.4,\n    wall_thickness=2.4,\n    base_thickness=3.0,\n    clip_length=12.0,\n    tab_length=10.0,\n    screw_hole_width=4.2,\n    draft=False,\n):\n    \"\"\"A screw-down clip: the bundle drops into an open-top channel, one screw holds it.\n\n    bundle_diameter: how thick the cable bundle is across\n    cable_clearance: how much wider than the bundle the channel is cut\n    wall_thickness: how thick each channel wall is\n    base_thickness: how thick the floor under the cable is, and the mounting tab\n    clip_length: how far the clip runs along the cable\n    tab_length: how far the mounting tab sticks out past the wall\n    screw_hole_width: how wide the screw hole through the tab is\n    \"\"\"\n    channel_width = bundle_diameter + cable_clearance\n    channel_depth = bundle_diameter\n    body_width = channel_width + 2 * wall_thickness\n    body_height = base_thickness + channel_depth\n\n    corner = (Align.MIN, Align.MIN, Align.MIN)\n\n    body = Box(body_width, clip_length, body_height, align=corner)\n    # Open at the top and at both ends: the cable lies along Y through the whole part.\n    channel = Box(channel_width, clip_length + 2, channel_depth + 1, align=corner).translate(\n        (wall_thickness, -1, base_thickness)\n    )\n    tab = Box(tab_length, clip_length, base_thickness, align=corner).translate((body_width, 0, 0))\n\n    screw_x = body_width + tab_length / 2\n    screw_y = clip_length / 2\n    screw = Cylinder(\n        screw_hole_width / 2,\n        base_thickness + 2,\n        align=(Align.CENTER, Align.CENTER, Align.MIN),\n    ).translate((screw_x, screw_y, -1))\n\n    solid = (body - channel) + tab - screw\n\n    if draft:\n        return solid\n\n    bed = solid.bounding_box().min.Z\n    concave = set(concave_edges(solid))\n\n    def keepable(e):\n        bb = e.bounding_box()\n        if e in concave:\n            return False\n        # Nothing lying in the bed face: a chamfer there buys nothing and slivers.\n        if bb.max.Z <= bed + TOL:\n            return False\n        # Nothing on the channel: its floor stays one flat face and its walls stay\n        # square, because the bundle sits against them.\n        if (\n            bb.min.X >= wall_thickness - TOL\n            and bb.max.X <= wall_thickness + channel_width + TOL\n            and bb.min.Z >= base_thickness - TOL\n        ):\n            return False\n        # Nothing on the screw hole: a lead-in there is fit geometry, not polish.\n        reach = max(\n            abs(x - screw_x) + abs(y - screw_y)\n            for x in (bb.min.X, bb.max.X)\n            for y in (bb.min.Y, bb.max.Y)\n        )\n        if reach <= screw_hole_width + TOL:\n            return False\n        return True\n\n    keep = solid.edges().filter_by(keepable)\n    return polish(solid, keep, CHAMFER)\n","userModified":false}}

{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5","id":"msg_011Cdeqf8JkxEPxuYNiC8wdd","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_01CuFwFSCrZ6eujfrhgqm8GL","name":"Write","input":{"file_path":"/var/folders/s4/by90nw7j7_l_nvvqs3hd9mjh0000gn/T/nurb-eval-trial-foh7nmqk/project/parts/cable_clip.md","content":"# cable_clip\n\n## What it is\n\nA screw-down clip for a cable bundle. The bundle drops into an open-top channel that\nruns the full length of the part, and a flat tab off one wall takes a single screw into\nwhatever the clip mounts to. It prints as modelled: flat bottom on the bed, no supports,\nnothing floating.\n\n## Design notes\n\nEverything is derived from `bundle_diameter`, which is the measured 8.0mm across the\ntaped bundle. The channel is `bundle_diameter + cable_clearance` wide, so 8.4mm at the\nmeasured size: 0.4mm of slack is enough for the bundle to drop in without being\nsqueezed, and little enough that it does not rattle. Channel depth is the bundle\ndiameter itself, 8.0mm, so the bundle sits fully below the wall tops rather than\nbulging out and pushing the walls apart.\n\nWalls are 2.4mm, six passes of a 0.4mm nozzle, and the 3.0mm base under the channel is\nwhat the screw clamps against, so it is the one place worth more than the wall\nthickness. Length along Y is 12.0mm, which is enough bearing on the cable to keep it\nfrom twisting under the clip without turning a cable tie into a bracket.\n\nThe tab is 10.0mm out from the outside of the right-hand wall, flush with the bottom\nand the same 3.0mm as the base, so the whole underside is one flat bed face. The 4.2mm\nhole is centred in the tab, leaving 2.9mm of material out to the end face and 3.9mm to\neach side, all of it well over the printer's minimum. `min_wall` fires at 2.9mm here if\nthe hole drifts off centre, which is how the first build was caught: `Cylinder(...,\nalign=Align.MIN)` aligns the bounding box, not the axis, so the hole came out one radius\noff in both X and Y and left 0.80mm of wall at the tab end. The hole is aligned\n`Align.CENTER` in X and Y for that reason.\n\nOverall 23.2 x 12.0 x 11.0mm.\n\nPolish is the standard 1.0mm chamfer, on the vertical corners and on the edges that run\nalong the cable. What it deliberately leaves out is in `## Don't` — the exclusions are\nthe whole of the polish pass on a part this small.\n\n## Don't\n\n- **Don't chamfer anything on the channel.** The floor stays one flat face the full\n  8.4mm width and both walls stay square for their full 8.0mm height, because that is\n  what the bundle beds against. The polish pass excludes every edge inside the channel\n  box by coordinate rather than by naming faces, so it survives a change in\n  `bundle_diameter`.\n- **Don't chamfer the cross edges at the two ends** (the horizontal edges running along\n  X at y=0 and y=12). On the wall tops that edge *is* the channel mouth, and a lead-in\n  at a mating mouth is forbidden outright; it also clips a 1mm triangle off the top\n  corner of each channel wall, which is a chamfer inside the channel by another name.\n  On the tab it is worse than useless: those corners already carry a vertical chamfer\n  and a top chamfer, and a third one meeting them leaves a 0.87mm2 facet. With the\n  cross edges left sharp the part has zero sliver faces, so the card needs no\n  `[accepted] sliver` line at all — the six triangles the doctrine would have let us\n  declare simply do not exist.\n- **Don't chamfer the screw hole.** A countersink or a lead-in there is fit geometry for\n  whatever screw goes through it, not polish, and it is not ours to guess.\n- **Don't put a fillet in the channel's inside corners** to relieve stress. The load\n  here is a screw pulling the base down against a flat surface, not a cantilever; there\n  is no bending moment at those corners to relieve, and a fillet would lift the bundle\n  off the floor and shrink the effective channel.\n- **Don't tilt this part for printing.** Every face is already vertical, horizontal or a\n  45 degree chamfer, nothing overhangs, and the load path never wraps a corner, so\n  `stand()` would only spend a visible corner for nothing.\n- **Don't round `bundle_diameter` to a tidy number.** It is a measurement and lives in\n  `measurements.toml`. Change the clearance if the fit is wrong, not the measurement.\n\n## Changelog\n\n- 2026-08-02: First version.
